title: Supplemental Property Tax Bills: A California Buyer's Guide
description: Got a surprise property tax bill after buying in California? Here's what a supplemental tax bill is, why impounds usually skip it, and how to plan ahead.
keywords: supplemental tax bill after buying a home
image_alt: A young man at a kitchen table reading a letter with a bill in the morning

faq.q: What is a supplemental property tax bill in California?
faq.a: It's a one-time bill that collects the difference between the previous owner's assessed value and your new base year value, prorated from the month after your purchase to the end of the fiscal year on June 30.

faq.q: Does my impound account pay the supplemental tax bill?
faq.a: Usually not. County assessors note that supplemental bills are typically paid directly by the new owner. Check with your loan servicer to confirm how they handle it.

faq.q: Why did I get two supplemental tax bills?
faq.a: If you took ownership between January 1 and May 31, you'll usually receive two: one for the rest of the current fiscal year and one for the following year, because that year's annual roll was already set on the old value.

faq.q: When does the supplemental tax bill arrive?
faq.a: Typically several months after escrow closes. Due dates vary, so follow the dates printed on the bill rather than the regular installment calendar.

body_html:
A few months after closing, the boxes are unpacked, the mortgage payment is on autopay, and a property tax bill shows up in the mail. Most new owners assume it's a mistake. Your lender is supposed to handle the taxes, right? Your escrow account is set up for exactly that.

Here's the part almost nobody explains at the closing table: in California, that bill is often real, it's often yours to pay directly, and it isn't covered by your impound account. It's called a supplemental property tax bill. With first-installment property taxes coming due right now across Southern California, this is the week a lot of recent buyers get confused, so let's walk through it.

What a Supplemental Property Tax Bill Actually Is

Under Proposition 13, a property's assessed value generally resets when it changes hands. The new value, called the base year value, is set at the market value on the date you took ownership. The Orange County Assessor puts it plainly: a reassessable change in ownership "establishes a new base year value for the property that equals the market value of the property at the time of transfer" (OC Assessor).

The catch is timing. The regular annual tax bill for the current fiscal year (July 1 through June 30) was already calculated on the previous owner's value. If you bought for more than that value, the county needs a way to collect the difference for the months you own the home. That's the supplemental bill: a one-time catch-up on the gap between the old assessed value and your new one, prorated to the end of the fiscal year.

Placer County describes the math simply: the supplemental tax is "computed from the 1st of the month following the change to the end of the fiscal year" (Placer County). The bigger the gap between what the seller's value was and what you paid, the bigger the bill. In Southern California, where many sellers have owned for decades, that gap can be large.

Why Your Impound Account Usually Doesn't Pay It

This is the source of most of the surprise. When you have an impound (escrow) account, your lender collects a portion of your property taxes each month and pays the regular bills. But that account was set up using the tax figures available at closing, which were based on the previous owner's value.

The Orange County Assessor is direct about it: supplemental bills are "typically paid by the new owner directly and are not included in impound accounts" (OC Assessor). The same page suggests calling your lender to confirm your impound account has enough to cover the higher ongoing taxes, too.

So there are really two adjustments coming:

  • The one-time supplemental bill, which you typically pay yourself.
  • A higher regular tax bill going forward, once your new value hits the annual roll. That usually shows up as an impound shortage at your lender's annual escrow analysis, which can raise your monthly payment.

Neither means anything went wrong. I go over the impound side in more detail in Closing Costs Explained.

When the Bill Arrives (and Why You Might Get Two)

Supplemental notices don't come right away. According to the OC Assessor, notices and bills are "mailed several months after escrow closes," and the bill itself arrives within about two weeks of the Notice of Supplemental Assessment (OC Assessor). That delay is why it feels random.

Your closing date also decides how many supplemental bills you get:

If you closed between...What to expect
June 1 and December 31Usually one supplemental bill, covering the rest of the current fiscal year
January 1 and May 31Usually two supplemental bills, one for the rest of the current fiscal year and one for the next, because the annual roll for that next year was already set on the old value

Orange County notes that ownership changes "between January 1 and May 31 are subject to two supplemental assessments," and San Luis Obispo County's assessor pamphlet explains the same rule (SLO County Assessor). Due dates on supplemental bills vary, so read the bill itself rather than assuming it follows the regular calendar.

Don't Mix It Up With the Regular Bill Due Now

November is when this gets confusing, because the regular annual bill is also in play. In Orange County, the first installment of secured property taxes is due November 1 and becomes delinquent after December 10, with a 10% penalty if it isn't paid by then. The second installment is due February 1 and becomes delinquent after April 10 (OC Treasurer-Tax Collector). Other Southern California counties use the same statewide schedule.

If you bought this year, a few things are worth checking this month:

  1. Find out who's paying the regular bill. If you have an impound account, your lender typically pays it. If you don't, it's on you, and the bill may still be mailed in the previous owner's name if the sale was recent.
  2. Look up your parcel on your county tax collector's website. You can see every bill tied to the property, including supplemental bills you may not have received yet.
  3. Separate the two bill types. A supplemental bill is labeled as such. Don't forward it to your lender expecting it to be paid from impounds unless your servicer has confirmed they handle it.
  4. Calendar the due dates printed on each bill. Penalties on late property taxes are steep and avoidable.

The Homeowners' Exemption and Other Things to Watch

If the home is your primary residence, file for the homeowners' exemption. It isn't automatic. San Luis Obispo County's pamphlet notes it can reduce the assessed value on a supplemental bill by up to $7,000 if the property wasn't already receiving it, and that claims filed within 30 days of the notice date get the full benefit (SLO County Assessor). Your county assessor usually mails the claim form after a sale, but check rather than wait. Deadlines and procedures can vary by county.

A few other points that come up often:

  • Supplemental bills can go the other way. If your purchase price was lower than the prior assessed value, you may get a refund instead. Orange County notes a supplemental refund takes roughly two to three months. Placer County notes the annual bill still has to be paid as originally billed (Placer County).
  • You can question the value. The notice explains how to request a review if you believe the assessed value is wrong, and the window is short.
  • Moving at 55 or older? Proposition 19 may let you carry your existing tax base to a new home, which changes the supplemental picture entirely. See Prop 19 Explained.
  • Taxes and deductions are a tax question. Whether and how property taxes affect your income taxes depends on your situation, so talk with a tax professional.

The Takeaway: Plan for It Before You Close

The best time to deal with a supplemental bill is before you get it. I'd rather buyers set money aside at the start than be surprised in month four.

Ask your loan officer or escrow officer to estimate your property taxes on the new purchase price, not the seller's current tax bill. Many county assessor websites offer a supplemental tax estimator. Then treat the estimated supplemental amount like a closing cost that just arrives late: park it in savings and leave it alone.

Agents can help here, too. A one-line heads-up in the closing email ("expect a supplemental tax bill in a few months, and it's usually not paid by your lender") saves clients a lot of stress and builds trust long after the deal closes.

A supplemental bill isn't an error or a penalty. It's California catching your taxes up to the price you paid. Expect it a few months after closing, expect to pay it directly, and expect your regular bill and impound payment to adjust afterward. File your homeowners' exemption if it's your primary residence, and watch the December 10 and April 10 deadlines.

If you're buying in Southern California and want to see a realistic estimate of your full housing cost, including taxes on the new value, reach out. I'd rather you know the whole picture before you sign.
